title: Why one low tide is lower
teaches: The Moon's tilt, the tide as a sum of regular waves, Kelvin's tide-predicting machine, and why summer's lowest tides come in daylight
summary: **Seattle's two daily tides are unequal.** Most days have a lower low and a higher low, often several feet apart, and the two highs differ too.

**The Moon's tilt makes the difference.** The Moon swings up to about 28° north and south of the equator, which tilts the bulges so that Seattle meets deep water on one side of the Earth and shallow on the other.
**The difference comes and goes every two weeks.** It is biggest when the Moon is furthest north or south and almost gone when it crosses the equator, a cycle separate from springs and neaps.
**Two steady waves of nearly equal period add to an uneven pattern.** They drift in and out of step, so the sum swells and shrinks over days.
**The tide is a sum of constituents.** Each is a steady wave: M2 (12.42 h) and S2 (12 h) twice a day; K1 (23.93 h), O1 (25.82 h) and P1 (24.07 h) once a day.
**The daily waves split the lows.** K1 with O1 carries the Moon's tilt and K1 with P1 the Sun's; at Seattle the daily waves are about as big as the twice-daily ones, which makes its tide mixed.

**Kelvin measured the tide instead of solving it.** Laplace's equations could not be solved for real seas, so Kelvin took each constituent's size and timing from a port's gauge record and in 1872 designed a machine that added them.
**Tide tables are still made this way.** Machines did it with pulleys and a wire until the 1960s; computers now add the same waves.
**Summer's lowest lows come in daylight at Seattle.** The Sun's daily wave keeps to the clock and flips between June and December, so winter's lowest lows come at night.

blocks.text: In late May 1792 George Vancouver's two ships lay at anchor in Puget Sound while Lieutenant Peter Puget took two boats south for a week, through the Tacoma Narrows and into the inlets of the South Sound, camping on the beaches at night. Anyone who hauls boats up a beach twice a day learns this sea's habit quickly: of the two low tides each day, one goes out much further than the other.

Seattle's tide table shows it plainly. The table counts heights from a zero set near the lowest water of an ordinary day (the last part of this lesson says exactly where), so a minus height is an unusually low tide. One stretch in mid-June can run like this: a high of about 11 feet in the early morning, a low of minus 3 feet at lunchtime, a high of 12 feet in the evening, and a low of only 7 feet at about 2 the next morning. Those two lows, about thirteen hours apart, differ by 10 feet. A week later the same table shows the two lows nearly equal.

Lesson 8 built the two bulges: the Moon pulls the near side of the Earth a little harder than the centre, and the centre a little harder than the far side, so the ocean stretches into a bulge facing the Moon and another facing away. The Earth turns under both, which gives two high tides and two low tides each day. If Seattle passed through both bulges in the same way, its two tides would be equal. Before reading on, it is worth trying to think what could make Seattle's trip through one bulge different from its trip through the other.

The Moon does not stay over the equator. Its orbit is tilted, so the Moon swings north of the equator, back across it, south, and back again, a round trip of 27.3 days. Its angle north or south of the equator at any moment is its **declination**. At the far point of each swing the declination reaches about 28° in these years, and less in others.[^standstill] The bulges point toward the Moon and away from it, so when the Moon is far north the bulge facing it is tilted up into the northern hemisphere, and the bulge on the far side is tilted down into the southern.

Now follow Seattle as the Earth turns. Seattle sits at about 47.6° north, and the Earth's turning carries it once a day around its **circle of latitude**, the ring of all places 47.6° north. With the bulges tilted, that ring passes close to the middle of the bulge facing the Moon, which is tilted toward Seattle's latitude, and half a day later far above the middle of the opposite bulge, which is tilted into the southern hemisphere. So Seattle meets deep water on one side of the Earth and only the thin upper edge of the bulge on the other: one high tide is high, and the other barely rises. Newton saw this effect of the tilt in 1687, in the same book as the bulges.

blocks.caption: The Earth seen side on, with the Moon to the right and the water's two bulges drawn far thicker than life. Seattle's dot goes round its circle of latitude once a day; it is filled while on the side of the Earth facing you. The lower panel is the water over Seattle through one turn, in Newton's picture: compare its two high points.
blocks.task: Tilt the Moon to 20° or more, north or south, and compare the two high waters in the lower panel

blocks.text: The Moon crosses the equator twice in each 27.3-day swing, once going north and once going south. Each time, the bulges are not tilted, Seattle passes through both at the same depth, and the two tides of the day are nearly equal. About a week later the Moon is at its furthest north or south and the difference is greatest. So the difference vanishes and returns about every two weeks. This is a separate clock from lesson 8's springs and neaps, which follow the Moon's phase from new to full, a 29.5-day cycle; because the two clocks run at slightly different rates, they slide past each other through the year.

At Seattle the difference shows mostly in the lows, with a smaller one in the highs. Newton's picture puts it all in the highs. The bulges only describe the pull, the **forcing**. The real ocean cannot take up that shape at once; the pull sets off waves that take hours to travel round the ocean basins and up the Strait (lesson 10 follows one into the Sound). The once-a-day part of the answer and the twice-a-day part reach Seattle with different delays, and the next parts show how a delay moves the difference from the highs to the lows.

Start with two plain waves, each rising and falling at its own steady rate. Add them together, hour by hour. If they have exactly the same period they stay in step and the sum is a single bigger wave. If one is slightly slower, it drops a little further behind on every cycle, so for a while the two crests coincide and the sum swings widely, then the crests fall opposite the troughs and the sum is small, and then they come back into step.

blocks.caption: Top: wave A rises and falls every 12 hours; wave B every so many hours, which you set. Both are shown over three days. Bottom: A plus B over a whole month, so the slow swelling and shrinking shows.
blocks.task: Set wave B to 12.42 hours and count the days between big swings in the lower panel

blocks.text: Nothing in either wave changes, yet their sum looks irregular. The closer the two periods, the longer they take to drift apart and back. At 12 and 12.42 hours, wave B falls 0.42 hours further behind on every cycle, and it takes about 12.42 ÷ 0.42, nearly 30, cycles of 12 hours to fall a whole wave behind and come back into step: about 355 hours, or 14.8 days. Those are the Sun's and the Moon's twice-daily waves, and the pattern is the spring and neap cycle of lesson 8, seen as two steady waves adding.

The same trick works the other way round: a tide that looks tangled can be pulled apart into steady waves, each with a period fixed by some cycle of the Moon or the Sun. Each of these waves is called a **constituent**. Five carry most of the tide at Seattle, and this lesson uses no others:[^names]

blocks.title: Seattle's five main constituents (about)
points: [[M2|moon]]: the Moon's twice-daily wave, every 12.42 hours, about 1.07 m (3.5 ft) high.
[[S2|sun]]: the Sun's twice-daily wave, every 12 hours, about 0.26 m (0.9 ft).
[[K1|moon]]: a daily wave every 23.93 hours, from the tilt of both the Moon and the Sun, about 0.83 m (2.7 ft).
[[O1|moon]]: a daily wave every 25.82 hours, from the Moon's tilt, about 0.46 m (1.5 ft).
[[P1|sun]]: a daily wave every 24.07 hours, from the Sun's tilt, about 0.26 m (0.9 ft).

blocks.text: The three daily waves are the tilt, written as steady waves. The Moon's tilt makes a once-a-day rise and fall that is strong while the Moon is far north or south and fades as it crosses the equator. A daily wave that swells and fades like that is exactly what two steady daily waves of slightly different period make when they add, as the twice-daily pair did above. For the Moon those two are K1 and O1, which fall in and out of step every 13.66 days: one peak with the Moon far north, one with it far south, in each 27.3-day swing.[^pair] The Sun's tilt works the same way over a year, through K1 and P1. K1 serves both because its period, 23.93 hours, is the time the Earth takes to turn once against the stars, which the Moon's and the Sun's tilt effects share.

Lay a once-a-day wave on top of a twice-a-day wave and, of the two lows in a day, one lands where the daily wave is also low, so it goes deeper; the other lands where the daily wave is high, so it is held up. Whether the split shows in the lows or the highs depends on when the daily wave peaks compared with the twice-daily one. That timing comes from how the Pacific, the Strait and the Sound respond, and it is measured rather than worked out (the next part tells how); at Seattle it puts most of the split in the lows. The figure starts with no daily waves at all. Before moving anything, guess what happens to the two lows of a day as K1 and O1 grow.

blocks.caption: A model of the tide over two weeks of May. M2 and S2 start at Seattle's sizes; K1 and O1 start at zero, as if the Moon and Sun never left the equator, and go up to 2 m. Dots mark the lows. The Seattle button sets all four to Seattle's values.
blocks.task: Guess, then raise K1 and O1 (or lower M2 and S2) until some day has only one low

blocks.text: Push the daily waves far enough and the held-up low climbs until it merges into the high beside it, and that day has one low and one high. One number sums up the balance: the **form number**, K1 plus O1 divided by M2 plus S2. Under about a quarter, the daily waves hardly show and a place has two nearly equal tides a day, as most of the Atlantic coast of North America does. Over about three, the daily waves win and most days have one high and one low, as along parts of the Gulf of Mexico. Seattle's is (0.83 + 0.46) ÷ (1.07 + 0.26), close to one: a **mixed** tide, two tides a day and strongly unequal, with the lower low the one beach walkers wait for.

Knowing the periods is not enough to predict a tide. A constituent's size and timing at a port depend on how the oceans, the Strait and the Sound answer the pull, and that is a question about water moving in real basins. In 1775 and 1776 the French mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace wrote down the equations for it: the ocean as a thin layer on a spinning Earth, set moving by the Moon and Sun, its tide a wave rather than a bulge standing still. They were right, and nobody could solve them for oceans with real coasts and depths.[^laplace]

The way round came from Glasgow. From 1867 [[William Thomson]], later Lord Kelvin, led a committee of the British Association that gave up on deriving each port's tide from first principles and measured it instead. Take a long record of hourly heights from a tide gauge, a year if possible. For each known period, find the size and timing of the steady wave hidden in the record: this is **harmonic analysis**. Then to predict the tide for any day in the future, add those waves back together. The arithmetic was the problem: a year of hourly predictions for one port meant nearly 9,000 additions of a dozen or so waves, each worked out by hand.

So in 1872 Kelvin designed a machine to do the adding. Each constituent got a crank that turns once per period, set to its port's timing, and on the crank a pulley that rises and falls by that constituent's size. A single wire is fixed at one end, runs over the first moving pulley, under a fixed one, over the next moving pulley, and so on, and carries the pen at its free end. When a moving pulley rises it takes up a loop of wire, which pulls the free end and lifts the pen; when it falls it gives the wire back. Each pulley's movement passes straight along the wire, so the pen moves by the sum of all of them and draws the tide on a roll of paper as the handle turns.

blocks.caption: A tide-predicting machine with Seattle's four largest constituents. Each crank turns at its own constituent's rate, the wire over the pulleys adds their movements, and the pen draws the sum on paper that moves to the left.
blocks.task: Turn the handle through two days

blocks.text: The first machine, built in 1872 and 1873, had ten cranks and could draw a year of tides for a port in a few hours. Others followed in several countries. The US Coast and Geodetic Survey's Tide Predicting Machine No. 2, a brass machine that added 37 constituents, made the country's tide tables, Seattle's among them, from about 1912 until the mid-1960s, when electronic computers took over the same sums.[^brass] The counts differ because more constituents only refine the sum: the four or five largest give Seattle's tide its shape, and the small ones adjust it by inches.

blocks.caption: From Newton's bulges to the tide tables.

events.label: US Machine No. 2 makes the tables

blocks.text: Today's Seattle tide table is still a sum of steady waves, each measured from the gauge on the Seattle waterfront. What the sum cannot include is weather: a deep low or a strong south wind can lift the water a foot or more above the prediction, which lesson 10 picks up.

The zero of the tide tables, promised at the start, is **mean lower low water**: the average, over many years, of the lower of each day's two lows.[^datum] A low below it is a **minus tide**, and the lowest of them uncover sea stars, moon snails and eelgrass that are under water most of the year. Seattle's naturalists plan their summer around them, and in June and July the best come in the middle of the day. In December and January the same deep lows come in the middle of the night.

The Moon's tilt cannot explain that, because the Moon's tides come about 50 minutes later each day: while the Earth turns once, the Moon moves on along its orbit, and the Earth needs extra time to catch up. Something tied to the Sun must be at work. The Sun's path is tilted too, north of the equator in June and south in December, and its tilt makes a once-a-day wave of its own through K1 and P1. Unlike the Moon's, this wave keeps to the clock, rising and falling at the same time of day for weeks on end. When the Sun crosses to the other side of the equator the wave flips: its highs and lows trade places, so its low moves by twelve hours. At Seattle, in the months around June, its low lands near midday by the Sun (a little after 1 pm on a summer clock), and any lunar low that falls near then is made deeper still. Around December its low lands near midnight.

blocks.caption: A model year at Seattle, from five constituents (M2, S2, K1, O1, P1): each dot is a day's lowest low, at its time of day. The bigger blue dots are minus tides. They gather around noon from spring to late summer and around midnight in winter. Times are sun time: noon is when the Sun is highest, a little after 1 pm on a Seattle summer clock.

blocks.text: The deepest minus tides come in runs of a few days, when a spring tide and the Moon's far swing north or south come together, and on each day of a run the low comes about 40 to 50 minutes later than the day before. The two cycles, 14.8 and 13.7 days long, line up about every six months, and the timing works out near the solstices, because at new or full moon near a solstice the Moon is near the Sun's own far north or south position. That is why June and December have the deepest runs, and enough to plan a low-tide walk from the table alone.

blocks.title: Outdoors: a minus tide
points: Look up the Seattle station on NOAA's tide predictions for May, June or July, and find a run of days with a low of minus 2 feet or lower in daylight.
Go to Constellation Park in West Seattle, Lincoln Park or the North Beach at Discovery Park an hour before the predicted low.
Mark the water's edge with a stick every ten minutes. Note when the water stops falling, and how far the beach runs out compared with an ordinary afternoon's low.

blocks.caption: Six questions on unequal tides
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why are the two low tides of a day at Seattle often very different in depth?
choices: The Moon's tilt tilts the bulges, so Seattle meets deep water on one side and shallow on the other
The Sun's bulge and the Moon's bulge pass Seattle at different hours on most days of the month
The ebb runs out through Admiralty Inlet faster on one tide than the other each day
items.why: With the Moon far north or south, the bulges are tilted. Seattle's circle of latitude passes near the middle of one and far from the middle of the other, so the two tides of the day differ.

items.ask: The Moon is crossing the equator this week. What does that do to the difference between Seattle's two daily tides?
choices: It makes the difference greatest, since the Moon pulls hardest on the equator
Nothing: the difference follows the Moon's phase, from new to full
items.why: With the Moon over the equator the bulges are not tilted, so Seattle passes through both at the same depth. The difference is greatest about a week later, when the Moon is furthest north or south.

items.ask: A tide record looks irregular: big swings for a few days, then small ones. What could produce that from waves that never change?
choices: Two steady waves of slightly different period drifting in and out of step
One steady wave whose period lengthens and shortens through the month
A single wave reflected back and forth until it dies away
items.why: Two steady waves add to big swings when their crests coincide and small ones when crest meets trough. The tide is a sum of such constituents, which is why it can be predicted.

items.ask: Why did Kelvin's method predict tides when Laplace's equations could not?
choices: It took each wave's size and timing from the port's own gauge record
Kelvin's machine solved Laplace's equations with pulleys, one basin at a time
Kelvin corrected an error in Laplace's equations, which then solved by hand
items.why: Harmonic analysis reads each constituent's size and timing from the record, which already contains the ocean's response. Predicting is then only adding the waves, which the machine did.

items.ask: At one port K1 plus O1 is five times M2 plus S2. What tide do people there see on most days?
choices: One high and one low a day
Two highs and two lows a day, all nearly equal
Two highs and two lows a day, with very unequal highs
items.why: With the daily constituents that strong, the second low of most days climbs into the high beside it and disappears. A form number above about three means a once-a-day tide.

items.ask: Why do Seattle's lowest summer tides come in daylight while winter's come at night?
choices: The Sun's tilt makes a daily wave that keeps to the clock and flips between June and December
Long summer days warm the water, and the warm water shrinks back by afternoon
The Moon stands higher in the summer sky, so its lows come in the daytime
items.why: The Moon's tides come about 50 minutes later each day, but the Sun's daily wave keeps clock time. With the Sun north in June its low falls near midday at Seattle; with the Sun south in December its highs and lows trade places, and its low falls near midnight.

standstill.title: How far the Moon swings
standstill.text: The Moon's furthest swing north and south changes over an 18.6-year cycle, from about 18° to about 28.5°. It was at its widest around 2024 and 2025, and will be at its narrowest in the early 2030s. Wider swings mean bigger differences between the two daily tides.

names.title: Why the odd names
names.text: The labels come from the nineteenth-century tables of harmonic analysis: M for the Moon, S for the Sun (*sol*), while K, O and P are only letters. The number counts crests a day, 2 for twice-daily waves and 1 for daily ones. NOAA uses 37 constituents for Seattle's predictions; the five in this lesson carry most of the range, and the figures that add waves use four or five of them.

pair.title: One swelling wave, or two steady ones
pair.text: A daily wave whose size rises and falls every 13.66 days is the same, by a rule of trigonometry, as two steady waves with periods of 23.93 and 25.82 hours added together. Tide tables use the steady pair because steady waves are easy to measure and to add.

laplace.title: Laplace's equations today
laplace.text: Laplace could solve his equations only for an idealised ocean covering the whole globe at an even depth. Computers now solve them for the real oceans, and since the 1990s satellites that measure the height of the sea surface have checked the results against the open-ocean tide measured from space. Harbour tide tables still come from harmonic analysis of each port's own gauge.

brass.title: Old Brass Brains
brass.text: Machine No. 2 was nicknamed Old Brass Brains. It was designed at the Coast and Geodetic Survey by Rollin Harris and E. G. Fischer. NOAA still keeps it.

datum.title: The zero of a tide table
datum.text: Mean lower low water is averaged over a 19-year period, the National Tidal Datum Epoch, long enough to take in the Moon's 18.6-year cycle. Charts give depths below the same zero, so a sailor adds the tide table's height to the charted depth to get the water under the keel.
